title: Trump Jr. warns Democrats want to “make Ohio a state” on the eve of a tight Ohio vote
dek: Closing out the GOP campaign near Toledo, Donald Trump Jr. slipped while reaching for the party’s line on D.C. statehood. The clip spread within the hour. Ohio, a state since 1803, votes Tuesday in two races rated close.
body:
On the last afternoon of the 2026 midterm campaign, standing in an airport hangar outside Toledo, Donald Trump Jr. told an Ohio crowd what he said Democrats would do with power: “They want to pack the Supreme Court. They want to make Ohio a state” [1][2]. He then added “make D.C. a state,” which appears to be the line he meant to deliver, and moved on [1][4]. Ohio has been a state since March 1, 1803 [3][6].

The slip came at a rally meant to give Republicans a final push in two Ohio races that forecasters rate as close, a Senate special election and an open governor’s seat, with polls opening Tuesday morning [4][8]. Within minutes of a clip being posted, the line was everywhere online [3][5].

## What was said, and where

The rally was held Monday, November 2, in the general aviation terminal hangar at Eugene F. Krantz Toledo Express Airport in Swanton, just west of Toledo. It was hosted by the Trump 47 Committee as part of Vice President JD Vance’s final-days swing for Republican candidates [1]. Trump Jr. appeared alongside Vance to rally support for Vivek Ramaswamy, the party’s nominee for governor, and Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to Vance’s old Senate seat in January 2025 and is running to keep it [4][9].

The passage came as Trump Jr. laid out what he described as the stakes of a Democratic Congress. In the fuller version transcribed by several outlets, he said Democrats want to pack the Supreme Court, make Ohio a state, make D.C. a state and “have permanent one-party rule” [2][3]. He went on to say that he did not know how it works, but that Democrats could do such things and get away with them in the name of preserving democracy, and that they were saying so openly and running on it [2][3].

The Irish Star’s account says that after a short pause he appeared to look back at the teleprompter before saying “make D.C. a state” [4]. The Akron Beacon Journal, in a piece republished by Yahoo News, likewise described the follow-up as an apparent self-correction [1]. Neither Trump Jr. nor the campaign had issued a clarification by Monday evening, according to the summaries of the clip circulating on X [5].

## How it spread

The clip came from C-SPAN’s coverage of the rally and was posted to X by Aaron Rupar, the independent journalist, after which it became a trending topic on the platform [5]. Aaron Parnas, a political commentator with a large following on Instagram and Threads, posted the same moment with a caption saying Trump Jr. claimed Democrats would make “Ohio a state” [7].

Reaction ran mostly to jokes. Crooks and Liars collected responses from Ron Filipkowski of MeidasTouch News, The Atlantic’s Jonathan Chait and others, most of them playing on the idea of a campaign against something that happened more than two centuries ago [3]. A widely shared post on X said Trump Jr. was campaigning against an event 223 years old [5]. The Irish Star noted the arm-waving delivery many viewers read as an impression of his father [4]. The substance of the closing argument around the slip was unchanged: the courts, D.C. statehood and which party controls Congress [2][4].

## Ohio is a state — with an asterisk

Ohio was the 17th state admitted to the Union, on March 1, 1803, with Chillicothe as its first capital [6]. But Trump Jr. is not entirely alone in historical confusion over the date. As the state prepared to celebrate its 150th anniversary in 1953, officials found that Congress had never passed a formal resolution admitting Ohio. Congress then passed one, and President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed it, declaring Ohio a state retroactive to March 1, 1803 [3][6]. Crooks and Liars cites the Ohio History Connection for the same history [3].

That technicality has nothing to do with Monday’s remark. Every account of the rally treats the line as a verbal slip for the District of Columbia, the statehood question that actually is part of the campaign debate [1][4][6].

## The real statehood argument

Washington, D.C., is a federal district created under the Constitution. It has a nonvoting delegate in the House and no senators [1]. Democrats in the House have passed bills to admit most of the district as a state, and statehood remains a plank for many Democrats. Republicans argue the push is about political advantage: a new state would very likely send two Democrats to the Senate and add a Democratic House seat, which is why GOP speakers pair it with expanding the Supreme Court as examples of what they call efforts to lock in one-party rule [1][2]. Supporters of statehood counter that the district’s roughly 700,000 residents pay federal taxes and serve in the military without full representation in Congress.

Trump Jr.’s line, before and after the slip, was a version of that Republican argument, delivered to a state whose two biggest races will help decide which party controls the Senate and how a large swing state is governed [2][4].

## The races Ohio decides Tuesday

The Senate contest is a special election for the rest of the term Vance won in 2022, running to January 2029. Husted, the appointed Republican incumbent, faces Sherrod Brown, the Democrat who held Ohio’s other Senate seat for 18 years before losing in 2024 [9]. Donald Trump carried Ohio by about 11 points in 2024 [9]. All three major forecasters, Cook, Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Inside Elections, rate the race a toss-up [9].

The governor’s race is open because Gov. Mike DeWine is term-limited. Ramaswamy, the businessman and former presidential candidate, won the Republican primary with President Trump’s endorsement and faces Amy Acton, the former state health director who led Ohio’s early pandemic response [9]. Cook and Sabato rate that race Lean Democratic; Inside Elections calls it a toss-up [9].

The last polls have shown Democrats ahead in both, mostly within or near the margin of error. A New York Times/Siena College poll released November 1 had Brown at 49 percent to Husted’s 44, and Acton at 49 percent to Ramaswamy’s 43, among likely voters, with a margin of error of 4.4 points [8][9]. Other late polls were closer: YouGov had Brown ahead 50 to 48 and Acton 52 to 46, InsiderAdvantage had Brown up 49 to 47 and Acton up 49 to 46, and ActiVote found both races essentially even [9]. In early October, Newsweek’s roundup found most public polls favoring the Democrats, with only Co/efficient showing both Republicans narrowly ahead [10].

President Trump has campaigned in the state for both Republicans, with rallies in Vandalia on October 3 and Chillicothe on October 28 [1][10]. Monday’s Swanton event in northwest Ohio was the ticket’s last big stop in the state before the vote [1][4].

## What to watch

Polls in Ohio close at 7:30 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday [9]. The Watch’s Election Desk will follow the count through the night and will report race calls only from the Associated Press or the state’s certification, never on its own [9].

Whether a single slip on a closing-day stage matters to any Ohio voter is doubtful; most voters have made up their minds by the final day, and many Ohioans have already voted early. What it did do was put the campaign’s last Ohio rally in front of a national audience that might not otherwise have noticed it, in two races close enough that both parties spent their final day in the state [4][5][8].
